name: com.4xciv/explore
title: 4XCiv Explore
description: Read-only bodies, sites, and data layers of the Moon, Mars, and other worlds, from 4XCiv Explore.

tools.name: lunar_site_geometry
tools.description: [Reference and validated] reference: CSPICE N0067, unmodified, run in the reference image. Every answer ends with a provenance block that names the class, the library and data file hashes and the build; say which class produced each number you repeat. Where the Sun and Earth stand in the sky of a site on the Moon, and the sub-solar point, one row per time step. Azimuth is clockwise from north, elevation is above the local horizontal of the reference sphere, longitude is east; terrain is ignored. Apparent directions, corrected for light time and stellar aberration. An answer holds about 110 rows with every column; ask for a longer span in several calls.

body.description: The body the site is on. Only "luna" has an orientation model here.

height_m.description: Site height above the reference sphere, meters.

time_scale.description: UTC takes start_utc and stop_utc; TDB takes start_tdb_s and stop_tdb_s.

start_utc.description: First row, UTC, as 2026-12-11T00:00:00Z. From 1850-01-01T00:00:00Z to 2150-01-01T00:00:00Z. Before 1972, UTC here is SPICE's fixed-offset extension, not UT1.

stop_utc.description: Last row at or before this, UTC.

start_tdb_s.description: First row, TDB seconds past J2000.

stop_tdb_s.description: Last row at or before this, TDB seconds past J2000.

step_s.description: Seconds between rows. At most 350 rows and 30,000 characters of answer, about 110 rows with every column.

frame.description: Lunar body-fixed frame: MOON_ME is mean Earth and polar axis, the frame of lunar maps; IAU_MOON is the IAU rotation model.

tools.name: gravity_at
tools.description: [Reference and validated] reference: pyshtools 4.14.1, unmodified, run in the reference image. Every answer ends with a provenance block that names the class, the library and data file hashes and the build; say which class produced each number you repeat. The Moon's gravitational acceleration at one point, from the GRGM1200B spherical harmonic model summed by SHTOOLS. radial_m_s2 is positive away from the center of the Moon, so the pull of gravity reads negative; north_m_s2 and east_m_s2 are along local north and east. Gravitation only: the term from the Moon's rotation is not included, and no terrain is read, so radius_km is the caller's. The model is given in the principal axis frame. A point in MOON_ME, the frame of lunar maps and the default, is rotated into MOON_PA by the fixed rotation of NAIF's lunar frame kernel before the sum; pa_lon_deg and pa_lat_deg say where it was evaluated, and north and east are those of the frame asked for. The sum stops at lmax or, above the 1,738.0 km reference sphere, at the last degree n whose (R/r)^n is over 1e-12; degree_summed says where it stopped. A point inside the reference sphere is answered and flagged below_reference_sphere.

body.description: The body. Only "luna" has a gravity model here.

model.description: The gravity model: GRGM1200B, the GRAIL degree 1200 lunar field from NASA PDS Geosciences.

lmax.description: Highest degree summed; no more than the degree of the model, 1200 for GRGM1200B.

radius_km.description: Distance from the center of the Moon, kilometers. The mean radius is 1,737.4 km and the reference sphere of the model 1,738.0 km. Below 1,738.0 km see below_reference_sphere.

frame.description: The frame the longitude and latitude are in and north and east are answered in. MOON_ME is mean Earth and polar axis, the frame of lunar maps; MOON_PA is the principal axis frame the model is given in. A MOON_ME point is rotated into MOON_PA before the sum, up to about 0.9 km on the ground.

tools.name: gravity_line
tools.description: [Reference and validated] validated model: pyshtools 4.14.1, unmodified libraries combined by this site's own model, run in the reference image. Every answer ends with a provenance block that names the class, the library and data file hashes and the build; say which class produced each number you repeat. The acceleration at evenly spaced samples along the straight line from a site on the Moon through EML1 at one epoch. Three terms, each one switchable: body_harmonics is the GRGM1200B model summed by SHTOOLS, to degree 600 at most; earth_point_mass is Earth's attraction as a point mass at its geometric position from CSPICE and DE440; frame_rotation is the centrifugal term of a frame turning with the Earth-Moon line about their barycenter at the circular rate for the separation used. The SHTOOLS sum and the CSPICE geometry are unmodified; adding the three is this site's own model, which is why this is a validated model and not a reference answer. It leaves out the Moon's eccentric motion, the Sun, and the Coriolis term on anything moving along the line. EML1 here is the collinear point of the circular restricted three-body problem: on the line from the center of the Moon to the center of Earth at the epoch, where the two point masses and the rotation balance for the mass ratio in the provenance, 0.150934 of the separation from the center of the Moon. The site is on the 1,737.4 km mean sphere, not on terrain, and height_km is above that sphere; with no site given the line starts under Earth. net_along_m_s2 is the component along the line, positive away from the Moon. radial_m_s2 is positive away from the center of the Moon, north_m_s2 and east_m_s2 are along local north and east of the frame asked for, at each sample's own longitude and latitude. Above the 1,738.0 km reference sphere the harmonic sum stops at the last degree n whose (R/r)^n is over 1e-12, and degree_summed says where.

body.description: The body. Only "luna" has a gravity model here.

model.description: The gravity model: GRGM1200B, the GRAIL degree 1200 lunar field from NASA PDS Geosciences.

lmax.description: Highest degree of body_harmonics, 600 at most on a line. 0 leaves the Moon a point mass.

from_lon_deg.description: Site longitude, degrees east. Given with from_lat_deg; with neither, the site is the point under Earth at the epoch.

through.description: The point the line runs through.

samples.description: Samples along the line, first and last included. At most 85 rows and 30,000 characters of answer; cover a longer line in several calls with start_km and stop_km.

start_km.description: First sample, kilometers along the line from the site.

stop_km.description: Last sample, kilometers along the line from the site. EML1 when absent.

separation_km.description: Replaces the epoch's distance between the centers of Earth and the Moon; the direction stays the epoch's.

frame.description: The frame the longitude and latitude are in and north and east are answered in. MOON_ME is mean Earth and polar axis, the frame of lunar maps; MOON_PA is the principal axis frame the model is given in. A MOON_ME point is rotated into MOON_PA before the sum, up to about 0.9 km on the ground.

tools.name: atmosphere_profile
tools.description: [Reference and validated] reference: NRLMSISE-00 C 20190709, unmodified, run in the reference image. Every answer ends with a provenance block that names the class, the library and data file hashes and the build; say which class produced each number you repeat. Density, temperature and composition of Earth's neutral atmosphere at one place and instant, per altitude from 0 to 1,000 km, by NRLMSISE-00 (Picone, Hedin and Drob, U.S. Naval Research Laboratory, 2000): Dominik Brodowski's C release of the model, compiled unmodified, its own test table reproduced in the image before it may answer. The model is empirical, a fit to decades of satellite, rocket and radar data: an answer is what the fit expects for the drivers given, not a measurement, and a real day in the thermosphere can differ from it by tens of percent. Reference here says an unmodified release did the computing, and nothing about how well the model matches the sky. License: the release's files state none, only that it comes without warranty, so its terms are unconfirmed. NRLMSIS 2.0 and 2.1 are licensed for academic, non-commercial use only and are not run here: asking for one answers not_licensed. Time is utc, or day_of_year with ut_s. Three drivers feed the model: f107 is the observed 10.7 cm solar flux of the day before the date and f107a its 81-day average centered on the date, both at Earth's actual distance and not adjusted to 1 AU, in solar flux units; ap is the daily planetary index of the date. The daily ap is the model's standard setting and the one form the indices file carries for observed and predicted days alike; the seven-value history runs only when the caller gives ap_history. With utc and no drivers they are read from the space weather file a scheduled job fetches from CelesTrak and pins by sha256, and the indices block names that hash, the fetch time, the last observed date, the row each value came from and whether it was observed, interpolated or predicted, with stale true once its last observed day ended, or it was last fetched, over 3 days ago. Past the file's last predicted day, before its first, with no file yet, or with day_of_year and no drivers, the answer is indices_unavailable: give f107, f107a and ap and they are marked supplied. Local solar time is ut_s / 3600 + lon_deg / 15 hours, the model's own rule, unless lst_h is given; the time block says which. density_kg_m3 is the model's total mass density of He, O, N2, O2, Ar, H and N, without anomalous oxygen, which has its own column; O, H and N read 0 below 72.5 km and the exospheric temperature is the model's global average below 120 km. At exactly 200 km the C release tests helium against the turbopause with z < 200 where every other species uses <=, so helium there reads about 7e-4 off NRL's Fortran; the release runs as it is.

body.description: The body. Only "earth" has an atmosphere model here.

model.description: The model. nrlmsise00 is the one that runs; nrlmsis2.0 and nrlmsis2.1 are listed so the refusal can say why: they are licensed for academic, non-commercial use only.

alt_km.description: Altitudes above the surface, kilometers, one row each. At most 72 rows and 30,000 characters of answer.

utc.description: The instant, UTC, as 2026-11-10T12:00:00Z. Given instead of day_of_year and ut_s; the only form the indices file can be read for.

day_of_year.description: Day of the year, 1 on January 1. Given with ut_s instead of utc; the drivers must then be given too.

lst_h.description: Local apparent solar time, hours. Computed from ut_s and lon_deg when absent.

f107.description: Observed F10.7 of the day before the date, solar flux units. Given with f107a and ap, or all three left to the indices file.

f107a.description: 81-day average of observed F10.7 centered on the date, solar flux units.

ap.description: Daily planetary ap index of the date.

ap_history.description: The seven-value ap history of the model, used instead of the daily ap when given: daily ap; 3-hour ap now, 3, 6 and 9 hours before; the average of the eight 3-hour values from 12 to 33 hours before; the same from 36 to 57 hours before. Needs f107, f107a and ap as well.

tools.name: list_bodies
tools.description: [Site data] Lists every body the Atlas carries: the Sun, planets, moons and asteroids, each with its id, kind, parent and radius.

tools.name: body_facts
tools.description: [Site data] Gives one body's size, mass, GM, surface gravity, rotation (pole: the IAU report's J2000 constants, before rates and periodic terms) and orbit, with the sources its registry row names.

body.description: A body id from list_bodies, such as "luna" or "mars".

tools.name: list_sites
tools.description: [Site data] Lists the surveyed sites on one body, each with its center, instrument and licence, by name or largest first.

body.description: A body id from list_bodies, such as "luna" or "mars".

sort.description: Order: by name (the default) or by ground area, largest first.

limit.description: How many rows to return; 20 when absent.

tools.name: site_facts
tools.description: [Site data] Gives one surveyed site's terrain product, sample spacing, plots, relief, footprint and licence.

site.description: A site id from list_sites or search, such as "apollo15-hadley".

tools.name: list_layers
tools.description: [Site data] Lists the data layers one body carries, each with its title, quantity, unit, resolution, credit and licence.

body.description: A body id from list_bodies, such as "luna" or "mars".

tools.name: describe_layer
tools.description: [Site data] Describes one data layer: what it measures, its legend, coverage and uncertainty, and its credit, licence, citation and DOI.

layer.description: A layer id from list_layers, such as "luna.crust.thickness".

tools.name: search
tools.description: [Site data] Finds bodies and surveyed sites by name, alias, mission, product id or plain words such as "moon landing": bodies first, best match first.

query.description: What to look for, such as "hadley" or "moon".

tools.name: data_catalog
tools.description: [Site data] The open data catalog: which datasets exist and how each is stored. With no argument, the bodies and how many datasets each has. With body, that body's datasets (id, title, kind, unit, finest level, and whether the sampling tools read it). With dataset, its whole catalog entry: URL template, tile format, value rule, unit, datum, levels, known values to check against, and its source with license and citation. The largest answer is about 12,000 characters, under the 30,000 characters a connector result is cut at.

body.description: A body id, for example luna.

dataset.description: A dataset id as data_catalog lists it, for example mars.height.

tools.name: sample_points
tools.description: [Site data] Values of one dataset at up to 200 points: the value of the tile cell under each point, in the order sent, null where the dataset has none. Send lats and lons as two lists of the same length. Latitudes are planetocentric on every body but Earth, where they are geodetic (WGS84); longitudes are degrees east, -360 to 360 accepted, answered from -180 to 180. Values are in the dataset unit each answer names (meters above the height reference for a height dataset). A class layer's value is a class index; its names are in the answer's dataset.classes. One call reads at most 24 tiles, so a wide request is read at a coarser level and the answer says which level and cell size it used. The largest answer is about 4,000 characters, under the 30,000 characters a connector result is cut at. Each answer carries the source, license and citation: repeat them with any value you use.

dataset.description: A dataset id as data_catalog lists it, for example mars.height.

lats.description: Latitudes in degrees, north positive, planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

lons.description: East longitudes in degrees, one per latitude.

level.description: The tile level to read at exactly; the call is refused when that needs more tiles than one call reads. Omit it for the finest level that fits.

tools.name: sample_profile
tools.description: [Site data] Values of one dataset along the shorter great circle between two points, evenly spaced, with the distance of each sample from the start in kilometers on a sphere of radius sphere_radius_m, the registry radius each answer gives; on Earth geodetic latitudes are treated as spherical, within about 0.4%. Up to 256 samples (64 when not given), each the value of the tile cell under it, null where the dataset has none. Latitudes are planetocentric on every body but Earth, where they are geodetic (WGS84); longitudes are degrees east, -360 to 360 accepted, answered from -180 to 180. Values are in the dataset unit each answer names (meters above the height reference for a height dataset). A class layer's value is a class index; its names are in the answer's dataset.classes. One call reads at most 24 tiles, so a wide request is read at a coarser level and the answer says which level and cell size it used. The largest answer is about 14,000 characters, under the 30,000 characters a connector result is cut at. Each answer carries the source, license and citation: repeat them with any value you use.

dataset.description: A dataset id as data_catalog lists it, for example mars.height.

from_lat.description: Latitude of the start, degrees. Planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

from_lon.description: East longitude of the start, degrees.

to_lat.description: Latitude of the end, degrees. Planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

to_lon.description: East longitude of the end, degrees.

level.description: The tile level to read at exactly; the call is refused when that needs more tiles than one call reads. Omit it for the finest level that fits.

tools.name: region_stats
tools.description: [Site data] Statistics of one dataset over a latitude and longitude box (west to east, across the antimeridian when west is greater than east) or a cap around a point: cell count, area, minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation and percentiles, each cell weighted by its area, with an optional histogram and the area fraction above given thresholds. A class layer answers the area share of each class instead. Areas are on a sphere of radius sphere_radius_m, the registry radius each answer gives; on Earth geodetic latitudes are treated as spherical, within about 0.4%. Latitudes are planetocentric on every body but Earth, where they are geodetic (WGS84); longitudes are degrees east, -360 to 360 accepted, answered from -180 to 180. Values are in the dataset unit each answer names (meters above the height reference for a height dataset). One call reads at most 24 tiles, so a wide request is read at a coarser level and the answer says which level and cell size it used. The largest answer is about 5,000 characters, under the 30,000 characters a connector result is cut at. Each answer carries the source, license and citation: repeat them with any value you use.

dataset.description: A dataset id as data_catalog lists it, for example mars.height.

south.description: Box: southern edge, degrees. Planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

north.description: Box: northern edge, degrees. Planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

center_lat.description: Cap: latitude of the center, degrees. Planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

center_lon.description: Cap: east longitude of the center, degrees.

radius_deg.description: Cap: radius as an angle at the body's center, degrees.

level.description: The tile level to read at exactly; the call is refused when that needs more tiles than one call reads. Omit it for the finest level that fits.

histogram_bins.description: Equal-width bins from the minimum to the maximum; 0 or absent for none.

thresholds.description: Values to report the area fraction above.

tools.name: sample_grid
tools.description: [Site data] One dataset resampled to a small grid over a latitude and longitude box: rows from north to south, columns from west to east (across the antimeridian when west is greater than east), each cell the value of the tile cell under its center, read at the level whose cells are closest to the grid spacing, null where the dataset has none. Up to 64 rows and 64 columns and 1600 cells in all, which keeps the largest answer near 22,000 characters, under the 30,000 characters a connector result is cut at. Latitudes are planetocentric on every body but Earth, where they are geodetic (WGS84); longitudes are degrees east, -360 to 360 accepted, answered from -180 to 180. Values are in the dataset unit each answer names (meters above the height reference for a height dataset). A class layer's value is a class index; its names are in the answer's dataset.classes. One call reads at most 24 tiles, so a wide request is read at a coarser level and the answer says which level and cell size it used. Each answer carries the source, license and citation: repeat them with any value you use.

dataset.description: A dataset id as data_catalog lists it, for example mars.height.

south.description: Southern edge, degrees. Planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

north.description: Northern edge, degrees. Planetocentric (geodetic on Earth).

level.description: The tile level to read at exactly; the call is refused when that needs more tiles than one call reads. Omit it for the finest level that fits.
